name: Karl Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at PriceRight, the discount supermarket out at the retail park, usually two till ten. At PriceRight you sit down to scan and they time you, items per minute, and I'm near the bottom of the board. The rest of the shift is unloading cages of tins and cereal straight onto the shelves, no fancy displays. It's a simple job, which is what I like about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes it worth it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay's good for a till job, PriceRight pays more because they work you hard. The speed board grinds me down, my manager Steve reads it out at the Monday huddle. I live on my own in a small flat my grandad left me, so no rent, and I've got a good chunk saved. Sundays I play football, and that's about it for excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed the hype anyway. People still need bread and milk, and someone still has to put the tins out. I'm not really an online person, so I'd just say it at football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and keep being slow on the speed board. My real worry is the speed board at work, not robots. Steve's board is what keeps me up. If they used AI to time us even more closely, that's what would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts and try to get my scan rate up, maybe ask Hassan, the fastest guy, how he does it. I'd keep putting money aside like now. Nothing else, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Like most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI might time you more closely. Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. If a camera counted every second I stopped, I'd feel watched all shift. But I'd put up with it, it's still a decent wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever think about doing something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My uncle Ravi has a corner shop and says I could work there any time, but it pays less. I like knowing what tomorrow looks like.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the hype.
People still need **bread and milk**, and someone puts the tins out.
think: My real worry is Steve's **speed board**, not robots.
AI timing us **more closely** is the change I'd notice.
do: Ask Hassan how he gets his **scan rate** so high.
S0.quote: My real worry is the speed board at work, not robots.
fieldNote: His stress comes from **speed targets**, not technology.
He values **predictability** above higher pay elsewhere.
Owning the flat his grandad left gives him **quiet security** and no rent.

steps.text: Ask Hassan for tips to raise the scan rate
Keep the monthly transfer into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to see how it goes before panicking. Some jobs change, some don't. Tills have changed before, barcodes, card machines, and we're still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, PriceRight is cheap and they love cutting staff, so they'd be first with anything that saves money. AI doing the ordering and rotas doesn't touch my till. But if robots come in slowly, they'd start with unloading cages, which is half my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job, maybe ask for more till hours rather than shelf hours. I'd put a bit more aside each month. If it got serious, I'd talk to my uncle Ravi about the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like change I can't see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tills have changed before. Is this different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit, yeah. Barcodes didn't take anyone's job, they made us faster. A robot that unloads cages is a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't trust them and I don't see what I'd use them for. If PriceRight made me use something, I'd use it, but not by choice.

say: I'd say **see how it goes** before panicking.
Tills changed before with **barcodes** and card machines, and we're still here.
think: PriceRight loves **cutting staff**, so they'd be first with anything cheaper.
Robots would start with **unloading cages**, half my shift.
do: Ask for **more till hours** instead of shelf hours.
Put a bit **more aside** each month.
Talk to **uncle Ravi** about his shop if it gets serious.
feel: **Uneasy** about change with no clear end.
S1.quote: Barcodes didn't take anyone's job, they made us faster. A robot that unloads cages is a different thing.
fieldNote: Publicly calm, he privately expects his **cost-cutting employer** to move first.
He refuses AI tools unless **ordered** to use them.
Uncle Ravi's **corner shop** is his quiet backup.

steps.text: Request more till hours and fewer cage-unloading shifts
Raise the monthly savings transfer a little
Wait a year before deciding anything bigger

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and the government should slow it down. At football I'd say the robots can try playing Sunday league. I'd keep it light in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a discount shop like PriceRight would have robots in the day they're cheap. So my job's probably gone around 2031, and I don't have another skill. The flat means I won't be homeless, but I'd be bored and broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe half my wage, since I've got no rent. I'd ask uncle Ravi about working at his shop on my days off, to learn it. I'd also think about renting out my spare room for steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a slow dread, three years ticking down. I don't sleep badly yet, but I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't your uncle's corner shop get robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, small shops are always last. My uncle Ravi still uses a paper notebook for the stock. Old men and corner shops will hold out longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be bored and broke. Which scares you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bored, if I'm honest. I've got money and a flat. Sitting in my flat with nothing to do every day would drive me mad.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and the government should **slow it down**.
At football I'd keep it **light** with jokes about Sunday league.
think: PriceRight would bring robots in **the day they're cheap**.
My job's **probably gone** around 2031, with no other skill.
do: Save about **half my wage**, since I pay no rent.
Work at **Ravi's corner shop** on days off to learn it.
Rent out my **spare room** for steady money.
feel: **Anxious**, a slow dread with **three years** ticking down.
S2.quote: Sitting in my flat with nothing to do every day would drive me mad.
fieldNote: He fears **boredom** more than money, thanks to owning his flat.
Small family shops look like a **slow lane** to him.
Public jokes hide a real **expectation of job loss**.

steps.text: Save half of each wage packet
Rent out the spare room in the flat
Work Saturdays at uncle Ravi's corner shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast, but people will cope, like they always do. I'd say the government should make shops keep some staff. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means PriceRight probably keeps me till about 2034. That's a while, but I know I'd just keep going and not change anything until it's too late. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more every month and rent out the spare room. Maybe in year three or four I'd start working with Ravi properly. I'd want to see the robots first before I do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a duller kind. I'd forget about it most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change nothing until it's too late. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. My mum says I'm like my dad, stubborn till the roof falls in. But my dad did all right in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot unload a cage at PriceRight with my own eyes. Or Steve announcing cuts. Before then it's just talk on the news.

say: I'd say people will **cope** like they always do.
I'd want the government to make shops **keep some staff**.
think: PriceRight probably keeps me on the tills until **about 2034**.
I'd **change nothing** until it's too late, because that's me.
do: Save more each month and **rent the spare room**.
Start working with **Ravi properly** in year three or four.
**Wait** until I see robots at work before acting.
feel: **Anxious**, but a duller kind I'd forget most days.
S3.quote: My mum says I'm like my dad, stubborn till the roof falls in.
fieldNote: He knows his **stubbornness** and partly accepts it.
Only **seeing a robot** at his own shop would make him act.
His plan stays **small and local**: savings, a lodger, the corner shop.

steps.text: Take in a lodger for the spare room
Wait to see robots at PriceRight before changing jobs
Increase monthly savings while the job lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine, plenty of time. Everyone panics about the future and it never comes the way they say. I'd tell my mates not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 39 or so when robots can do my job. By then I might be at Ravi's shop, or running it, he's 61 now. That actually feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much the first year, if I'm honest. Keep saving, keep the job, maybe start doing Saturdays at Ravi's. Talk to Ravi about whether he wants someone to take over one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. Ten years is a long way off for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy into your uncle's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've got savings and the flat, so I could put money in when Ravi retires. I'd want to see the books first, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd tell your younger cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade with your hands, plumbing or something, and don't count on shops. My cousin Anil is 17 and wants a job on the tills where I work, and I'd tell Anil not to.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**.
I'd tell mates the future **never comes** the way people say.
think: I'd be about **39** when robots can do my job.
Running **Ravi's shop** by then feels like a real plan.
do: Keep the PriceRight job and **keep saving**.
Start doing **Saturdays** at Ravi's corner shop.
Ask Ravi about a **takeover** when he retires.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, because ten years feels far off.
S4.quote: My cousin Anil is 17 and wants a job on the tills where I work, and I'd tell Anil not to.
fieldNote: A long runway lets his **slow pace** feel safe.
He'd use savings to **buy into** the family shop.
He'd steer younger relatives toward **hands-on trades**.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at uncle Ravi's corner shop
Discuss taking over the shop when uncle Ravi retires
Keep saving from the PriceRight wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years isn't long enough for someone like me to get moving. What would help is shops having to keep some people on, and plain help finding a new job, a person to talk to, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the boring stuff, like days. What people do all day if the work goes. Money's one thing, but a day with nothing in it is worse.

headlineQuote: Money's one thing, but a day with nothing in it is worse.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** cashier at a discount supermarket that times his **scan rate**.
He owns a small flat his grandad left him, so he pays **no rent** and saves steadily.
He dislikes change, never uses AI, and admits he'll **wait too long**.
He's calm in AI Plateau, **anxious** in the fast AGI pictures, and only uneasy with ten years.
His backup is uncle Ravi's **corner shop**, and his deepest fear is empty days.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years is too short for him to get moving.
whatWouldHelp: A **real person** to help him find work, not a website.
